blocks.text: Market Size
Private credit market size

blocks.html: Global private debt assets under management stand at US$2,548.6bn on PitchBook’s latest count (Exhibit 1). Institutional funds account for US$1,928.6bn (75.7%, as of 31 December 2025), retail vehicles for US$413.2bn (16.2%) and insurance balance sheets for an estimated US$206.8bn (8.1%), the latter two as of 30 June 2026. The mix is shifting. Institutional AUM fell by US$91.2bn from US$2,019.8bn at end-2024 — the first annual decline in the series, which starts in 2015 — while retail grew from US$287.5bn and insurance from US$137.5bn at end-2024. Growth is now coming from the wealth and insurance channels rather than from drawdown funds. PitchBook restated earlier years in this edition and the exhibit adopts the restated history.

blocks.text: Supply side

blocks.html: Dry powder fell to US$547.0bn at end-2025 from the 2024 peak of US$669.2bn, a drop of US$122.2bn in one year, while invested NAV rose by US$31.1bn to US$1,381.7bn (Exhibit 3). Dry powder is now 39.6% of NAV, down from 49.5% a year earlier and the lowest ratio in the series. Fundraising explains part of it. Institutional funds raised US$264.8bn across 292 funds in 2025 (2024: US$259.4bn across 416), and US$157.7bn across 89 funds in the first half of 2026, equal to 59.6% of the 2025 total (Exhibit 4). Capital raised is still below the 2021 peak of US$328.3bn, and the fund count is a fraction of the 579 closed in 2022: money is concentrating in fewer, larger vehicles. Morgan Stanley, using PDI data, puts first-half fundraising at about US$220bn, up 34% year on year, with the average direct lending fund at US$4.3bn. The supply of capital has not dried up; it has been drawn down faster than it has been replaced.

blocks.text: Demand side

blocks.html: Deal volume is the weak spot. KBRA-tracked direct lending origination totalled US$120bn in the year to July, down 23% year on year, and May’s US$8bn was the lowest month since late 2023 (Exhibit 5). The fall is concentrated in refinancing, down 47%; non-refinancing volume of about US$93bn is down 10%, and LBO financing of US$53bn is up 4%. On our three-month calculation non-refinancing deals were 82.6% of origination in July. New-money lending is therefore holding up better than the headline suggests; what has disappeared is the repricing and refinancing trade.

blocks.html: Private credit is also losing some share of buyout financing to the syndicated market. In 2Q26 it financed 39 LBOs against 15 in the syndicated market, a share of 72% by count and the first quarter below 80% since 3Q24; the trailing twelve-month share slipped to 81.4% from 83.8% (Exhibit 6). Banks are competing harder for new buyouts, but they are not yet taking out the existing private book.

blocks.text: Fund flow — middle-market CLOs

blocks.html: Middle-market CLOs remain the main term-leverage channel for direct lenders, and it is open. New issuance was US$17.77bn in the first six months of 2026, up 5.2% on the US$16.88bn of the same period in 2025, while BSL CLO issuance fell 26.2% to US$57.76bn; the middle-market share of new CLO supply rose to 23.53% from 17.75% (Exhibit 7). Full-year 2025 issuance was US$38.50bn. Liability costs are stable rather than falling: the average middle-market ‘AAA’ spread was 152bp in the first half against 159bp a year earlier, and its premium over BSL ‘AAA’ ended June at 22.1bp after 33.2bp in May. The clearest sign of tighter economics is in resets and refinancings, where middle-market volume fell 54.2% to US$11.78bn: managers are still printing new deals but are no longer able to cut the cost of old ones.

blocks.text: Returns & Relative Value
Direct lending returns versus public credit

blocks.html: Over 2015 to June 2026 private debt returned 7.8% a year with volatility of 2.1%, a Sharpe ratio of 3.6. High yield returned 5.4% with 7.9% volatility and single-B syndicated loans 5.3% with 6.4% (Exhibit 8). Morgan Stanley puts the return advantage over single-B loans at about 2.9pp a year. Two caveats apply. Private marks are appraisal-based and therefore smoothed, which flatters volatility and the Sharpe ratio; and the 82.4% correlation with syndicated loans says the underlying credit risk is largely the same. The return gap is real; the volatility gap is mostly an accounting one.

blocks.text: Private credit spread premium over syndicated loans

blocks.html: New-issue spreads have turned wider. The rolling 90-day unitranche spread reached 522bp in July from a trough of 490bp in February, while the single-B syndicated spread moved the other way, from 463bp to 431bp, leaving a premium of 91bp (Exhibit 10). PitchBook | LCD’s quarterly series tells the same story on a different basis: direct lending at 509bp and single-B loans at 332bp in 2Q26, a premium of 178bp against 122bp in 1Q26. The compression that defined 2024 and 2025 has stopped.

blocks.text: Pricing & Term
Spread

blocks.html: Three independent sources now place new direct lending deals in a 500–550bp range. J.P. Morgan describes spreads widening from tights of 475bp in late 2025 and early 2026 to 500–550bp; KBRA’s unitranche measure is at 522bp; and Guggenheim reports its own year-to-date closings at S+539 with first-lien net leverage of 4.2x (Fund Update). That is still well inside the 675–700bp peak J.P. Morgan records for this cycle, so pricing has improved from the lender’s side without yet reaching levels that signal stress.

Covenant structure and PIK

blocks.html: Documentation is where the upper middle market has given most ground. In S&P’s sample every lower middle-market deal of the 2021–2024 vintages carries at least one financial covenant and 79% of 2024-vintage core middle-market deals do, but only 26% of 2024-vintage upper middle-market deals — 74% are covenant-lite, up from 32% for the 2023 vintage (Exhibit 12). PIK toggles follow the same gradient: 41% of 2024-vintage upper middle-market deals have one, against 22% in the core and 5% in the lower middle market (Exhibit 13). S&P reports median leverage of 8.5x and median cash interest coverage of 1.5x for deals with a PIK toggle, and 22% of software deals carry one. The largest borrowers have the weakest documents and the most room to defer cash interest, which is the opposite of how the size premium in pricing is moving.

blocks.text: Credit Fundamentals
Default rate

blocks.html: On S&P’s measure defaults fell in the second quarter. The credit-estimate default rate including selective defaults was 3.93% in June, down from 4.79% in March, and conventional defaults — bankruptcies and missed payments — were 0.88%, against a US speculative-grade rate of 3.74% (Exhibit 14). The gap between the two credit-estimate lines is the story: S&P counts 125 distressed exchanges over twelve months against 29 conventional defaults, with PIK conversions (66%) and amend-to-extend transactions (48%) the main triggers. Compared with the syndicated market, direct lending defaults of 3.9% are below 4% for the first time in more than three years but still above the 2.8% in BSL (Exhibit 15).

blocks.text: Recovery rate

blocks.html: Marks on defaulted direct loans fall late and fast. Over the twelve months to July, BDC marks on loans that went on to default averaged 76.7 a year before default, 63.2 six months before and 55.0 three months before, reaching 45.9 at the default date; syndicated loans started lower at 70.7 and ended higher at 49.7 (Exhibit 20). The private market therefore recognises less of the loss in advance. By sector, average implied recoveries since 2023 range from 64.9 in building and construction to 41.6 in industrials, with software at 46.6 (Exhibit 21). These are marks at the point of default, not ultimate recoveries, which is how they sit alongside Morgan Stanley’s 70–80% assumption; the difference is the value lenders expect to recover by working the loan out, and it is an assumption rather than an observed number.

blocks.text: Leverage

blocks.html: Direct lending borrowers remain the most leveraged part of US leveraged credit at 5.7x gross debt to EBITDA, against 4.0x for syndicated loans and 3.6x for high yield (Exhibit 22). Provider medians range from 4.7x at KBRA to 7.1x at S&P, with Fitch at 5.9x and Lincoln at 5.2x, and neither of the two time series has moved this year (Exhibit 23). Morgan Stanley describes the typical borrower as a company with EBITDA of US$30–40m, 5–7x levered. Software stands out: S&P’s median leverage for software credit estimates is 8.1x against 7.1x for all sectors. Leverage is not rising, but it is not being worked down either.

blocks.text: Related news

items: Non-traded BDC redemption requests eased in the third quarter. Stanger data covering 19 BDCs (98% of the market) show requests of US$13.8bn, or 11.5% of NAV, down from 12.7% in the second quarter; about 40% was met, leaving US$8.2bn unmet against US$9.8bn a quarter earlier. Why it matters: the 5% quarterly caps are holding and the backlog is shrinking, but it is still large enough to keep these vehicles out of the new-deal market, which supports spreads on new commitments. Source: AltsWire, 2026-10-02

Fitch’s private credit default rate was 6.2% in October. That compares with 6.3% in September and keeps the rate at or above 6.0% since April. Bankruptcies alone account for 0.4%; PIK deferrals are 49% of default events and maturity extensions 38%. Software is at 0.6% against 9.8% for industrials. Why it matters: the series post-dates every default figure in this report and confirms a plateau, not an acceleration, made up almost entirely of restructurings. Source: ABF Journal, 2026-11-18

Capital is arriving faster than deals. PitchBook | LCD estimates third-quarter direct lending volume at US$49.77bn, down 28% year on year, while Preqin data show direct lending funds raised US$129.15bn in the first nine months, up 35% and the highest nine-month total in data back to 2016. In the quarter US$16.39bn of direct loans were refinanced into the syndicated market against US$2.60bn the other way. Why it matters: the spread widening in this report may not last if this imbalance persists. The article is a secondary citation of both sources. Source: M&A Alerts, 2026-10-22

The SEC proposed rules that widen retail access to private markets. The package would modernise the interval fund framework so that repurchase schedules can match portfolio liquidity, require disclosure of performance-based compensation, and seeks comment on accredited-investor routes that do not depend on wealth. It follows the 2025 executive order opening the near-US$14tn 401(k) market to private credit. Why it matters: the retail and insurance channels are where AUM growth now comes from, and these rules would extend that shift. Source: Alternative Credit Investor, 2026-10-01

The US midterm result puts the 401(k) route in doubt. Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Advisers quoted by Alternative Credit Investor say the wealth channel runs under existing SEC rules and is unaffected, but the Labor Department’s fiduciary safe harbour is still only a proposal, and one that could be reversed after 2028 may not persuade plan sponsors to adopt. Why it matters: the largest untapped pool of retail capital for private credit now carries political risk, which tempers the fundraising optimism in the item above. Source: Alternative Credit Investor, 2026-11-05

blocks.text: Things We Should Know

blocks.html: Five observations we consider important after reading all of this quarter’s materials — points that cut across the framework sections above and bear directly on the Junson portfolio:
blocks.text: Five observations we consider important after reading all of this quarter’s materials — points that cut across the framework sections above and bear directly on the Junson portfolio:

items: The software wall has been pushed out, not taken down. The share of software direct loans due in 2026–27 fell from 8.4% at the start of the year to 5.7%, but loans with less than three years to run reached a series-high 32% (Exhibit 31). Implication for Junson: Guggenheim PDF IV is our only software exposure, at 18% of par against about 30% for the twelve largest BDCs; we should ask the manager for the maturity profile of those loans by year.

Default rates and loss rates are now different conversations. S&P counts 125 distressed exchanges against 29 conventional defaults, and Morgan Stanley translates an 8% default forecast into 1.6–2.4% of losses. Implication for Junson: when a manager reports “no defaults”, the questions that matter are how many loans were amended, extended or switched to PIK, and at what mark.

The public–private BDC gap is largely about vintage. Public BDC non-accruals are 5.14% and private 1.79%, a gap of 3.3pp, and UBS reports non-accrual rates of 11% and 8% for the 2020 and 2021 vintages. Implication for Junson: our three funds are 2023 and 2024 vintages and should be benchmarked against young portfolios, not against the BDC average; clean numbers today are expected rather than a sign of outperformance.

Terms are improving for lenders deploying now. New-deal spreads are back in a 500–550bp range, non-traded BDCs are constrained by a US$8.2bn redemption backlog, and Guggenheim describes a lender-friendly reset after second-quarter volume fell 55% quarter on quarter. Implication for Junson: Guggenheim PDF IV and HSBC RCF are both still deploying, which is the right side of this trade; the risk is that record fundraising (US$129.15bn in nine months) competes the improvement away within a few quarters.

The rates view has turned against floating-rate borrowers. Goldman Sachs and UBS both flag higher-for-longer rates, and PAG notes that markets have moved to price possible increases in late 2026 or early 2027. Interest coverage of 2.1x leaves limited room. Implication for Junson: higher base rates raise income on all three funds but also raise default risk in the direct lending book; PAG’s bank-originated reference portfolios and HSBC’s senior revolvers are the better-protected positions if rates do rise.

items: Near-dated software paper is being pushed out. The share of software direct loans due in 2026–27 fell from 8.4% at the start of the year to 5.7% at 2Q26, and 2028 maturities from 18.9% to 16.7%, while 2033 maturities jumped from 1% to 8% as borrowers refinanced into new seven-year loans.

But the clock is still running. Sub-three-year maturities reached a series-high 32% of software direct loans at 2Q26, up from 17% at 1Q25, while sub-two-year maturities are contained at 10%. S&P estimates US$50bn of credit-estimated software loans mature by end-2028, down from US$60bn at end-2025.

Direct lending is more front-loaded than the syndicated market. About 21% of BDC assets are due by end-2028 against 17% of syndicated loans, and 6% of direct loans still mature in 2027 versus 2% in BSL; in CLOs, 34% of private credit CLO assets mature by 2028 against roughly 16% for BSL CLOs.

blocks.html: Fund snapshot
blocks.text: Fund snapshot

rows: Diversified portfolio of revolving credit facilities (RCFs) to sponsor-backed LBO borrowers with EBITDA > US$20m

items: Quarter activity. EUR 100m of additional investor commitments signed, taking fund size to EUR 434.8m; three investments made — Project Pique II (add-on), Project Aventa and Project Chalk, the latter two in settlement — for 14 investments held; no capital calls and a EUR 0.5m distribution on 22 June 2026.

Manager commentary. After a subdued start to 2026 the European leveraged finance market recovered in Q2, with June the strongest month of issuance in the past year; banks remain keen sellers of RCFs at a discount in the secondary market, which the manager says lets the fund capture OID and target mid-teens returns, and the near-term maturity wall is prompting refinancings that generate further RCF opportunities.

blocks.html: The fund reports a TVPI of 1.39x, a DPI of 0.20x and an IRR of 47.84% after fees and before carry, up from 1.21x, 0.14x and 34.50%. These figures need to be read against the capital base: only EUR 8.4m of the EUR 434.8m fund has been called, NAV is EUR 10.0m, and the strategy earns commitment fees and purchase discounts on facilities that are, on average, 10.6% drawn. A small denominator makes the multiples and the IRR look far stronger than a like-for-like comparison with a drawn fund would. The fund’s credit facility stood at EUR 8.8m, and every asset is on watchlist status Green.

blocks.html: Outstanding commitments total EUR 117.4m across 14 facilities, of which 12 are settled and 2 in settlement, and EUR 9.9m is drawn (Exhibit 46). Only three facilities were drawn at quarter-end — Emerald at 34%, Media at 49% and Oliver at 29% — which is the normal state for a revolver portfolio and the reason utilisation, rather than default, is the variable to watch: a sharp rise in drawings would be the early sign of borrower stress. The manager’s estimated return on invested capital ranges from 9.7% to 24.0% by facility. Two earlier facilities, Clark and Vision, have been realised, and after quarter-end the fund committed EUR 13.3m to a new project, Rio.
